rows.solution: Transposing swaps \(a_{ij}\) with \(a_{ji}\), so \(A' = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 3 & -8 \\ -3 & 0 & -5 \\ 8 & 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), which is exactly \(-A\). A matrix satisfying \(A' = -A\) is skew-symmetric, so A is a skew-symmetric matrix. The other three descriptions fail: it is not the null matrix, since it has non-zero entries; it is not symmetric, because \(a_{12} = -3\) while \(a_{21} = 3\); and it is not diagonal, because entries off the leading diagonal are non-zero. Note that the three diagonal entries are all \(0\), which is forced in any skew-symmetric matrix by \(a_{ii} = -a_{ii}\).

rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.figure: REQUIRED — the stem names no curve at all, so the question IS the printed graph. It shows several branches of the inverse-cotangent relation with horizontal dashed asymptotes at \(y = -\pi\), \(y = \pi\) and \(y = 2\pi\), the axis marked at \(\pm\pi/2\) and \(3\pi/2\), and the principal branch falling from near \(\pi\) through \((0,\ \pi/2)\) towards \(0\). Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
Read the shape of the graph rather than looking for a formula.
Every branch drawn is defined for all real \(x\), each branch is strictly decreasing, and all the asymptotes are HORIZONTAL lines — the x-axis together with the dashed lines \(y = -\pi\), \(y = \pi\) and \(y = 2\pi\). There is no vertical asymptote anywhere.
That rules out \(y = \cot x\) and \(y = \tan x\) immediately: both are periodic in \(x\) and have vertical asymptotes (at \(x = n\pi\) and \(x = (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2}\) respectively), so their graphs would be cut by vertical lines, not levelled off by horizontal ones.
Between the two inverse functions, \(y = \tan^{-1} x\) is INCREASING and confined between \(y = -\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(y = \frac{\pi}{2}\), which does not match. The branch through the middle of the picture falls from near \(y = \pi\) on the far left, passes through \(\left(0,\ \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), and tends to \(0\) on the far right — this is precisely the principal branch of \(\cot^{-1}\), whose range is \((0, \pi)\); the branches above and below it are the same curve shifted by multiples of \(\pi\).
Hence the graph depicts \(y = \cot^{-1} x\).

rows.stem: Let \(f(x) = x^2\), \(x \in R\). Then, which of the following statements is **incorrect** ?

options.label: A
options.text: Minimum value of f does not exist.

options.label: B
options.text: There is no point of maximum value of f in R.

rows.solution:
\(f(x) = x^2\) is a polynomial, so it is continuous and differentiable at every real number, in particular at \(x = 0\); both of those statements are therefore true. Since \(x^2 \to \infty\) as \(|x| \to \infty\), f is unbounded above and so attains no maximum anywhere on \(R\), making the statement about there being no point of maximum value true as well.
But \(f(x) = x^2 \ge 0\) for every real \(x\), with equality at \(x = 0\). So the minimum value \(0\) both exists and is attained: \(f'(x) = 2x\) vanishes only at \(x = 0\), and \(f''(0) = 2 > 0\) confirms a minimum there.
Hence the statement that is incorrect is 'Minimum value of f does not exist.'

rows.subtopic: Order and Degree of a Differential Equation
rows.stem:
The order and degree of the differential equation

\(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} + 4\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right) = x \log\left(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right)\)

are respectively :
rows.solution:
The ORDER of a differential equation is the order of the highest derivative appearing in it. Here that is \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), so the order is \(2\).
The DEGREE is the power of that highest derivative, but only once the equation has been written as a polynomial in the derivatives. In this equation \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) also appears inside \(\log\left(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right)\), a transcendental function of the derivative, and no algebraic rearrangement can free it. The equation can therefore never be expressed as a polynomial in its derivatives, so the degree is not defined.
Hence the order and degree are respectively '2, not defined'.

rows.stem: Chances that three persons A, B, and C go to the market are 30%, 60% and 50% respectively. The probability that at least one will go to the market is :
rows.solution:
Treat the three visits as independent events. We are given \(P(A) = 0\cdot3\), \(P(B) = 0\cdot6\), \(P(C) = 0\cdot5\), so the complements are \(P(A') = 0\cdot7\), \(P(B') = 0\cdot4\), \(P(C') = 0\cdot5\).
'At least one' is much easier through the complement — the single event that NOBODY goes:
\(P(\text{none goes}) = P(A')P(B')P(C') = 0\cdot7 \times 0\cdot4 \times 0\cdot5 = 0\cdot14\).
Hence
\(P(\text{at least one goes}) = 1 - 0\cdot14 = 0\cdot86 = \frac{86}{100} = \frac{43}{50}\),
which is the choice \(\frac{43}{50}\).
(The value \(\frac{7}{50} = 0\cdot14\) is the probability that none of them goes, and \(\frac{14}{10} = 1\cdot4\) exceeds \(1\), so it could not be a probability at all.)

rows.stem: Determine those values of x for which \(f(x) = \dfrac{2}{x} - 5\), \(x \ne 0\) is increasing or decreasing.
rows.solution:
Write \(f(x) = \frac{2}{x} - 5 = 2x^{-1} - 5\), so that
\(f'(x) = -2x^{-2} = \frac{-2}{x^2}\).
For every \(x\) in the domain we have \(x \ne 0\), hence \(x^2 > 0\) and
\(f'(x) = \frac{-2}{x^2} < 0\).
The derivative is therefore never zero and never positive: there is no interval anywhere on which f increases. So f is decreasing throughout its domain — strictly decreasing on \((-\infty, 0)\) and strictly decreasing on \((0, \infty)\), and it is increasing for no value of x.
[Note: the marking scheme records this simply as 'f is decreasing in its domain', which is the expected answer. It is worth adding that the domain \(R - \{0\}\) is not a single interval, so the conclusion has to be read on each of the two intervals separately: for instance \(f(-1) = -7\) is less than \(f(1) = -3\) even though \(-1 < 1\).]

rows.stem:
Find the value of \(\lambda\) if the following lines are perpendicular to each other :

\(l_1 : \dfrac{1 - x}{-3} = \dfrac{3y - 2}{2\lambda} = \dfrac{z - 3}{3}\)

\(l_2 : \dfrac{x - 1}{3\lambda} = \dfrac{1 - y}{1} = \dfrac{2z - 5}{3}\)
rows.solution:
Two lines are perpendicular exactly when the dot product of their direction ratios is zero, so first put each line into the standard symmetric form \(\frac{x - x_1}{a} = \frac{y - y_1}{b} = \frac{z - z_1}{c}\), in which the numerator of each fraction must be the variable itself minus a constant, with coefficient \(1\).
For \(l_1\): \(\frac{1 - x}{-3} = \frac{x - 1}{3}\), and \(\frac{3y - 2}{2\lambda} = \frac{3\left(y - \frac{2}{3}\right)}{2\lambda} = \frac{y - \frac{2}{3}}{\frac{2}{3}\lambda}\). So
\(l_1 : \frac{x - 1}{3} = \frac{y - \frac{2}{3}}{\frac{2}{3}\lambda} = \frac{z - 3}{3}\), with direction ratios \(\left(3,\ \frac{2\lambda}{3},\ 3\right)\).
For \(l_2\): \(\frac{1 - y}{1} = \frac{y - 1}{-1}\), and \(\frac{2z - 5}{3} = \frac{2\left(z - \frac{5}{2}\right)}{3} = \frac{z - \frac{5}{2}}{\frac{3}{2}}\). So
\(l_2 : \frac{x - 1}{3\lambda} = \frac{y - 1}{-1} = \frac{z - \frac{5}{2}}{\frac{3}{2}}\), with direction ratios \(\left(3\lambda,\ -1,\ \frac{3}{2}\right)\).
Setting the dot product to zero,
\(3(3\lambda) + \frac{2\lambda}{3}(-1) + 3 \cdot \frac{3}{2} = 0\)
\(\Rightarrow 9\lambda - \frac{2\lambda}{3} + \frac{9}{2} = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{25\lambda}{3} = -\frac{9}{2}\)
\(\Rightarrow \lambda = -\frac{27}{50}\).

rows.stem: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}\), are three matrices, then find ABC.
rows.solution:
A is of order \(1 \times 3\), B is \(3 \times 3\) and C is \(3 \times 1\), so the product ABC is defined and is a \(1 \times 1\) matrix. Matrix multiplication is associative, so it is convenient to compute \((AB)C\), which keeps every intermediate step a single row.
First,
\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 + 1 + 0 & 0 - 3 + 0 & 1 - 4 + 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -3 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\).
Then
\((AB)C = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -3 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} = 3(2) + (-3)(3) + (-3)(4) = 6 - 9 - 12 = -15\).
Hence \(ABC = \begin{bmatrix} -15 \end{bmatrix}\).

rows.stem: A coin is biased so that the head is 3 times as likely to occur as tail. If the coin is tossed three times, find the probability distribution of number of tails. Hence, find the mean of the distribution.
rows.solution:
'The head is 3 times as likely to occur as tail' means \(P(H) = 3P(T)\). Since \(P(H) + P(T) = 1\), this gives \(4P(T) = 1\), so
\(P(T) = \frac{1}{4}\) and \(P(H) = \frac{3}{4}\).
Let X be the number of tails in three independent tosses, so X takes the values \(0, 1, 2, 3\) and
\(P(X = r) = {}^{3}C_{r}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{r}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{3 - r}\).
Therefore
\(P(X = 0) = \left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{3} = \frac{27}{64}\),
\(P(X = 1) = 3 \cdot \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{9}{16} = \frac{27}{64}\),
\(P(X = 2) = 3 \cdot \frac{1}{16} \cdot \frac{3}{4} = \frac{9}{64}\),
\(P(X = 3) = \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{3} = \frac{1}{64}\).
As a check these add to \(\frac{27 + 27 + 9 + 1}{64} = \frac{64}{64} = 1\).
The mean is
\(\text{Mean} = \sum x\,P(x) = 0 + \frac{27}{64} + 2 \cdot \frac{9}{64} + 3 \cdot \frac{1}{64} = \frac{0 + 27 + 18 + 3}{64} = \frac{48}{64} = \frac{3}{4}\),
which agrees with the binomial formula \(np = 3 \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4}\).

rows.stem: Use integration to find the area of the region enclosed by curve \(y = -x^2\) and the straight lines \(x = -3\), \(x = 2\) and \(y = 0\). Sketch a rough figure to illustrate the bounded region.
rows.solution:
Sketch the region first. \(y = -x^2\) is a downward parabola with its vertex at the origin, so on \(-3 \le x \le 2\) the curve lies ON or BELOW the x-axis: it drops to \(y = -9\) at \(x = -3\), rises to \(y = 0\) at \(x = 0\), and falls again to \(y = -4\) at \(x = 2\). The region required is bounded above by the line \(y = 0\) (the x-axis), below by the curve, and at the sides by the vertical lines \(x = -3\) and \(x = 2\) — a region lying entirely below the x-axis, pinched to a point at the origin.
Because the curve lies below the axis the definite integral of \(y\) is negative, so the area is its modulus:
\(\text{Area} = \left|\int_{-3}^{2} (-x^2)\,dx\right| = \left|\left[-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-3}^{2}\right| = \left|-\frac{1}{3}\left(2^3 - (-3)^3\right)\right| = \left|-\frac{1}{3}\left(8 + 27\right)\right| = \frac{35}{3}\).
Equivalently, integrating the HEIGHT of the region, upper curve minus lower curve \(= 0 - (-x^2) = x^2\), gives the same value without any sign to chase:
\(\int_{-3}^{2} x^2\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-3}^{2} = \frac{8}{3} + \frac{27}{3} = \frac{35}{3}\).
So the required area is \(\frac{35}{3}\) square units.

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: Find the foot of the perpendicular drawn from point \((2, -1, 5)\) to the line \(\dfrac{x - 11}{10} = \dfrac{y + 2}{-4} = \dfrac{z + 8}{-11}\). Also, find the length of the perpendicular.
rows.solution:
Write the line in parametric form. Putting
\(\frac{x - 11}{10} = \frac{y + 2}{-4} = \frac{z + 8}{-11} = \lambda\),
any point Q on the line is \(Q = (10\lambda + 11,\ -4\lambda - 2,\ -11\lambda - 8)\), and the line has direction ratios \((10, -4, -11)\).
Let \(P = (2, -1, 5)\) be the given point and let Q be the foot of the perpendicular from P. Then
\(\overrightarrow{PQ}\) has direction ratios \((10\lambda + 11 - 2,\ -4\lambda - 2 + 1,\ -11\lambda - 8 - 5) = (10\lambda + 9,\ -4\lambda - 1,\ -11\lambda - 13)\).
Since PQ is perpendicular to the line, the dot product with \((10, -4, -11)\) is zero:
\(10(10\lambda + 9) + (-4)(-4\lambda - 1) + (-11)(-11\lambda - 13) = 0\)
\(\Rightarrow 100\lambda + 90 + 16\lambda + 4 + 121\lambda + 143 = 0\)
\(\Rightarrow 237\lambda + 237 = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = -1\).
Substituting \(\lambda = -1\), the foot of the perpendicular is
\(Q = (-10 + 11,\ 4 - 2,\ 11 - 8) = (1, 2, 3)\).
The length of the perpendicular is the distance PQ:
\(PQ = \sqrt{(1 - 2)^2 + (2 + 1)^2 + (3 - 5)^2} = \sqrt{1 + 9 + 4} = \sqrt{14}\).
So the foot of the perpendicular is \((1, 2, 3)\) and the length of the perpendicular is \(\sqrt{14}\) units.
